entry.title: [org.xerial.snappy:snappy-java] snappy-java: Heap buffer overflow in Snappy.uncompress*Array typed-array methods
entry.content:
Impact

Snappy.uncompressCharArray, uncompressShortArray, uncompressIntArray, uncompressLongArray, uncompressFloatArray and uncompressDoubleArray sized the result array by dividing the declared uncompressed byte length by the element size, but native code wrote the full byte length. If the declared length is not a multiple of the element size, up to 7 bytes are written past the end of the Java array, corrupting the heap.

Patches

Fixed in 1.1.10.9 (#739). These methods now reject uncompressed lengths that are not a multiple of the element size with SnappyIOException.

Workarounds

Check that Snappy.uncompressedLength(input) is a multiple of the element size before calling these methods.

References

  • https://github.com/xerial/snappy-java/security/advisories/GHSA-gwq9-9ffj-mvrv
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-93451
  • https://github.com/xerial/snappy-java/issues/729

entry.title: [org.xerial.snappy:snappy-java] Duplicate Advisory: snappy-java: Heap buffer overflow in Snappy.uncompress*Array typed-array methods
entry.content:
Duplicate Advisory

This advisory has been withdrawn because it is a duplicate of GHSA-gwq9-9ffj-mvrv This link is maintained to preserve external references.

Original Description

snappy-java through 1.1.10.8 contains a buffer overflow vulnerability in typed Snappy.uncompress*Array methods that allocate output arrays by dividing uncompressed length by element size but pass the undivided length to native code. Attackers controlling compressed input can cause misaligned length values to write past array bounds with attacker-controlled bytes, corrupting heap memory.

entry.title: [org.xerial.snappy:snappy-java] snappy-java: JVM crash from unchecked ranges in Snappy.arrayCopy and SnappyOutputStream.rawWrite
entry.content:
Impact

Snappy.arrayCopy(Object src, int offset, int byteLength, Object dest, int destOffset) called a native memcpy without validating the ranges. A negative or oversized byteLength or offset read or wrote outside the arrays and crashed the JVM. SnappyOutputStream.rawWrite and SnappyInputStream.rawRead, and therefore the typed-array write/read methods, pass caller-supplied ranges to this method.

Patches

Fixed in 1.1.10.9 (#741). Snappy.arrayCopy checks both ranges before copying. The stream read/write methods validate offsets and lengths, and reject typed-array ranges whose byte size overflows int.

Workarounds

Validate offsets and lengths before calling these methods.

References

  • https://github.com/xerial/snappy-java/security/advisories/GHSA-xqrx-qh46-34m7
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-116590

entry.title: [org.xerial.snappy:snappy-java] snappy-java: Unbounded memory allocation from attacker-declared uncompressed lengtha
entry.content:
Impact

Several decompression paths in snappy-java allocate an output buffer sized by the uncompressed length declared in the first bytes of the compressed data, before decompressing or validating it. A few bytes of crafted input can therefore force an allocation of up to 2 GB, causing OutOfMemoryError (denial of service), or a NegativeArraySizeException for declared lengths of 2^31 or more.

Affected entry points include Snappy.uncompress(byte[]), Snappy.uncompressString, the Snappy.uncompress*Array methods, SnappyInputStream, and SnappyFramedInputStream. The maxChunkSize limit added for CVE-2023-43642 bounds only the compressed chunk length, so it does not prevent this.

Patches

Fixed in 1.1.10.9 (#739). Snappy.uncompressedLength() now rejects negative declared lengths, and lengths larger than any valid Snappy stream of the given size can produce. The densest Snappy element expands 3 bytes to 64, so the limit is 64/3 of the compressed size. Allocations are therefore proportional to the input actually received.

Workarounds

Before decompressing untrusted data, check that Snappy.uncompressedLength(input) is within an application-specific limit.

References

  • https://github.com/xerial/snappy-java/security/advisories/GHSA-q233-g92q-qxp6

entry.content:
Duplicate Advisory

This advisory has been withdrawn because it is a duplicate of GHSA-q233-g92q-qxp6. This link is maintained to preserve external references.

Original Description

Xerial snappy-java before 1.1.10.9 contains an unbounded memory allocation vulnerability that allows attackers to exhaust JVM memory by declaring a large uncompressed length in compressed input. Attackers can supply a few crafted bytes to Snappy.uncompress, uncompressString, SnappyInputStream or SnappyFramedInputStream to force allocations up to 2 GB, causing OutOfMemoryError and denial of service.

entry.title: [org.codehaus.izpack:izpack-installer] IzPack has Path Traversal in UnpackerBase that allows writing files outside the installation directory via malicious pack entries
entry.content:
Summary

IzPack's UnpackerBase.unpack() resolves pack-file target paths without any canonical-path or directory-containment check. An attacker who distributes a trojanized installer JAR (the format is unsigned) can include pack entries whose targetPath contains ../ sequences. When a victim runs the installer the file is written to an attacker-chosen location on disk under the victim's privileges — including startup folders, PATH directories, or system locations.

Details

Vulnerable method: com.izforge.izpack.installer.unpacker.UnpackerBase.unpack() Source file: izpack-installer/src/main/java/com/izforge/izpack/installer/unpacker/UnpackerBase.java Vulnerable lines (5.2.4): ~618–627

The relevant code path is:

String targetPath = packFile.getTargetPath();             // attacker-controlled
String path       = IoHelper.translatePath(targetPath, variables); // separator swap ONLY
File   target     = new File(path);                       // no canonical check
// ... mkdirs() then file is written to `target`

IoHelper.translatePath() (source: izpack-util/.../IoHelper.java) performs only file-separator character conversion ('/' ↔ File.separatorChar) and contains no security validation whatsoever. There is no call to getCanonicalPath(), no startsWith(installDir) containment check, and no normalisation of .. segments.

Because IzPack installer JARs carry no digital signature, an attacker can repack any legitimate installer with malicious PackFile entries. The file format is a standard ZIP with serialised resources — no integrity protection.

Confirmed unpatched in HEAD (fetched from GitHub, 2025):

git show HEAD:izpack-installer/src/main/java/com/izforge/izpack/installer/unpacker/UnpackerBase.java \
  | grep -n 'getCanonicalPath\|startsWith.*install\|traversal'
# (no output — fix not present)

PoC

# 1. Clone IzPack source and view the vulnerable code directly
git clone --depth=1 --branch izpack-5.2.4 https://github.com/izpack/izpack.git
sed -n '615,650p' izpack/izpack-installer/src/main/java/com/izforge/izpack/installer/unpacker/UnpackerBase.java

# 2. Compile and run the following Java reproducer (no IzPack classpath needed):

// TestPathTraversal.java
import java.io.*;

public class TestPathTraversal {
    // Exact replication of IoHelper.translatePath() — separator swap, no security
    static String translatePath(String destination) {
        return destination.replace('/', File.separatorChar);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        String installDir   = "/tmp/izpack_install";
        String maliciousPath = installDir + "/../../../tmp/ESCAPED_FILE";

        // This is what UnpackerBase does:
        String path   = translatePath(maliciousPath);
        File   target = new File(path);           // resolves traversal
        target.getParentFile().mkdirs();
        try (FileWriter fw = new FileWriter(target)) {
            fw.write("Written outside install dir via IzPack path traversal\n");
        }
        System.out.println("File written to: " + target.getCanonicalPath());
        System.out.println("Inside installDir: " +
            target.getCanonicalPath().startsWith(new File(installDir).getCanonicalPath()));
    }
}

javac TestPathTraversal.java && java TestPathTraversal
# Output: File written to: /tmp/ESCAPED_FILE
#         Inside installDir: false

Impact

Any user who runs an IzPack-generated installer is affected. The attacker only needs to distribute a repackaged installer — a common social-engineering vector. On Windows (the primary IzPack platform) the victim typically runs the installer as a local administrator, so the attacker can write to %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup, %SystemRoot%\System32, or any other location reachable by the victim user. On Linux/macOS the same applies for user-writable locations.

No authentication, no special privileges and no interaction beyond running the installer are required on the victim side.

Credits

This issue was identified by Michał Majchrowicz, Marcin Wyczechowski, and Paweł Zdunek, members of the AFINE Team.

References

  • https://github.com/izpack/izpack/commit/4233ba38d0f1825f9cf3e0204e5261a5498e29d8

entry.title: [org.apache.tomcat.embed:tomcat-embed-core] Apache Tomcat - HTTP/2 no-authority bypass of strict SNI validation
entry.content:
Improper Input Validation vulnerability in Apache Tomcat due to incomplete fix for CVE-2026-32990.

This issue affects Apache Tomcat: from 11.0.20 through 11.0.24, from 10.1.53 through 10.1.57, from 9.0.115 through 9.0.120.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 11.0.25, 10.1.59 or 9.0.121, which fix the issue.

entry.title: [com.google.guava:guava] Google Guava: CompactHashMap/CompactHashSet/MapMakerInternalMap deserialization triggers uncontrolled memory allocation
entry.content:
CompactHashMap/CompactHashSet/MapMakerInternalMap native deserialization triggers uncontrolled memory allocation

Summary

CompactHashMap, CompactHashSet, and MapMakerInternalMap implement readObject(ObjectInputStream) by reading an attacker-controlled elementCount or initialCapacity from the stream. On the very first insertion during or after deserialization (for the CompactHash* collections, inside allocArrays()) or immediately during deserialization (for MapMakerInternalMap), the implementation eagerly allocates arrays sized to that full, unvalidated value (up to CompactHashing.MAX_SIZE = 2^30-1, ~1.07 billion, for example) before the rest of the stream's actual content has been consumed. A 72-byte malicious serialized stream containing a single tiny element can force a multi-gigabyte allocation and crash a JVM with OutOfMemoryError, dynamically confirmed against the current release.

Details

CompactHashMap.readObject() (guava/src/com/google/common/collect/CompactHashMap.java):

private void readObject(ObjectInputStream stream) throws IOException, ClassNotFoundException {
  stream.defaultReadObject();
  int elementCount = stream.readInt();
  if (elementCount < 0) {
    throw new InvalidObjectException("Invalid size: " + elementCount);
  }
  init(elementCount);
  for (int i = 0; i < elementCount; i++) {
    K key = (K) stream.readObject();
    V value = (V) stream.readObject();
    put(key, value);
  }
}

elementCount is only checked for being non-negative; there is no upper bound and no relationship enforced between the declared count and how much data actually follows in the stream. init(elementCount) (line 251) just stores the value (clamped to [1, CompactHashing.MAX_SIZE], i.e. up to 2^30-1):

void init(int expectedSize) {
  Preconditions.checkArgument(expectedSize >= 0, "Expected size must be >= 0");
  this.metadata = Ints.constrainToRange(expectedSize, 1, CompactHashing.MAX_SIZE);
}

The real allocation is deferred to allocArrays(), which fires lazily on the first put() call — i.e. after only one key/value pair has actually been read off the wire:

int allocArrays() {
  ...
  int expectedSize = metadata;
  int buckets = CompactHashing.tableSize(expectedSize);
  this.table = CompactHashing.createTable(buckets);
  setHashTableMask(buckets - 1);
  this.entries = new int[expectedSize];
  this.keys = new Object[expectedSize];
  this.values = new Object[expectedSize];
  return expectedSize;
}

With expectedSize near CompactHashing.MAX_SIZE (2^30-1), this single call allocates a hash table plus three expectedSize-length arrays — multiple gigabytes — triggered by a stream that has, at that point, only supplied one small real element. CompactHashSet.readObject()/allocArrays() have the identical shape. CompactLinkedHashMap/CompactLinkedHashSet extend these classes and inherit the same unguarded path.

The problem with MapMakerInternalMap is similar, with a size read from the serialized data and stored in a MapMaker instance for later user during deserialization, when the MapMaker is passed back to MapMakerInternalMap and segments are allocated by calling newSegment, whose implementations (example) create Segment instances (example) that allocate arrays of the requested capacity through the newTable helper.

This is the same amplification shape as the already-fixed CVE-2018-10237 (AtomicDoubleArray/CompoundOrdering: attacker declares a large size, library eagerly allocates before validating against actual stream content). That fix rewrote AtomicDoubleArray.readObject() to grow an ImmutableLongArray.Builder incrementally per element actually read, rather than pre-allocating from the declared size — Guava's own HashBiMap.readObject() documents the same defensive principle explicitly in a comment: init(16); // resist hostile attempts to allocate gratuitous heap. CompactHashMap/CompactHashSet do not follow either of these two patterns already present elsewhere in the same codebase.

Reachability: All classes are top-level, implements ... Serializable, and require no special classpath setup beyond Guava being present (near-ubiquitous on JVM backends). A native Java deserialization attacker names the class directly in a hand-crafted stream — no particular Guava factory method needs to have been used by the victim application, exactly as with the precedent CVE.

PoC

Full source and run instructions in the attached poc-guava-compacthash-dos.zip (Maven project, guava:33.7.1-jre — the current latest release — as the only dependency). The PoC:

  1. Uses reflection only to legitimately obtain a CompactHashSet instance (it is package-private; a real attacker does not need this step, since they craft the serialized bytes directly rather than calling Guava's own serialization code).
  2. Serializes one set with 1 element and one with 2 elements, diffs the two byte streams to locate the exact offset of the elementCount field (byte-precise, not guessed).
  3. Patches that one 4-byte field in the 1-element stream from 1 to 0x3FFFFFFF (CompactHashing.MAX_SIZE), leaving the rest of the 72-byte stream (one real "A" element) untouched.
  4. Feeds the resulting 72-byte malicious stream into a plain new ObjectInputStream(...).readObject() call against the real, unmodified guava-33.7.1-jre.jar.

Actual run output:

### -Xmx8g (generous heap) ###
Located size field at offset 63, value=1 (expected 1)
Malicious stream size: 72 bytes
Declared elementCount: 1073741823 (~1.07 billion)
Real payload: 1 tiny string element ("A")
=== RESULT ===
Exception: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
Time to allocate+fail: 4013 ms
Heap used before: 3 MB
Heap used after (at failure point): 4103 MB
JVM max heap (-Xmx): 8192 MB

### -Xmx128m (ordinary service-sized heap) ###
Located size field at offset 63, value=1 (expected 1)
Malicious stream size: 72 bytes
Declared elementCount: 1073741823 (~1.07 billion)
Real payload: 1 tiny string element ("A")
=== RESULT ===
Exception: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
Time to allocate+fail: 24 ms
Heap used before: 4 MB
Heap used after (at failure point): 2 MB
JVM max heap (-Xmx): 128 MB

A 72-byte input forces ~4.1 GB of real allocation before failing on an 8 GB heap, and crashes a 128 MB heap in 24 ms — over 50,000x amplification between input size and forced allocation.

To reproduce: mvn -q compile dependency:build-classpath -Dmdep.outputFile=cp.txt && java -Xmx128m -cp "target/classes:$(cat cp.txt)" poc.Poc

Impact

Uncontrolled resource consumption (CWE-770 / CWE-400) via native Java deserialization: any application that runs ObjectInputStream.readObject() on data reachable by an attacker, and has Guava on its classpath (true for a large fraction of the JVM ecosystem), can be crashed with a single ~72-byte payload, regardless of what type the application itself expected to deserialize.

Severity

CVSS 3.1: AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H — identical vector to CVE-2018-10237, the precedent this is a sibling of. Recomputed with the full formula: exploitability = 8.22×0.85×0.44×0.85×0.85 = 2.221; ISS = 1-(1×1×0.44) = 0.56; impact = 6.42×0.56 = 3.595; base = roundup(5.816) = 5.9 (Medium).

Affected

com.google.guava:guava, all editions (-jre/-android) — confirmed on the current latest release, 33.7.1-jre. CompactHashMap/CompactHashSet/CompactLinkedHashMap/CompactLinkedHashSet have had this same readObject/allocArrays shape for a long time (probably since they were added in Guava 23.6), and similarly for MapMakerInternalMap (which was introduced in Guava 4.0); not tested against older individual releases.

Suggested fix

Apply the same defense already used elsewhere in this codebase: either clamp the initial init() capacity to a small constant regardless of the declared elementCount (as HashBiMap.readObject() already does — init(16); // resist hostile attempts to allocate gratuitous heap) and grow incrementally as elements are actually read, or grow the backing arrays incrementally per iteration of the deserialization loop (as the fixed AtomicDoubleArray.readObject() does via ImmutableLongArray.Builder) instead of eagerly sizing to the full attacker-declared count on first insert.

  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-102554
  • https://github.com/google/guava/commit/b931fe9d6d5cf00bc55714ad3308d086f71850fe

entry.title: [org.apache.cxf:cxf-core] Apache CXF has Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference
entry.content:
Apache CXF's EndpointReferenceUtils and W3CMultiSchemaFactory classes construct a SAXParserFactory without the necessary JAXP hardening configurations, enabling out-of-band (OOB) external entity resolution. Users are recommended to upgrade to versions 4.2.2 or 4.1.7 or 3.6.12, which fix this issue.

entry.title: [org.apache.logging.log4j:log4j-core] Apache Log4j 1 to Log4j 2 bridge: silent log event loss in Log4j1XmlLayout due to unescaped XML 1.0 forbidden characters
entry.content:
The Log4j1XmlLayout from the Apache Log4j 1-to-Log4j 2 bridge fails to escape characters forbidden by the XML 1.0 standard, producing malformed XML output. Conforming XML parsers are required to reject documents containing such characters with a fatal error, which may cause downstream log processing systems to drop or fail to index affected records.

Two groups of users are affected:

  • Those using Log4j1XmlLayout directly in a Log4j Core 2 configuration file.
  • Those using the Log4j 1 configuration compatibility layer with org.apache.log4j.xml.XMLLayout specified as the layout class.

Users are advised to upgrade to Apache Log4j 1-to-Log4j 2 bridge version 2.25.4, which corrects this issue.

[!NOTE] The Apache Log4j 1-to-Log4j 2 bridge is deprecated and will not be present in Log4j 3. Users are encouraged to consult the Log4j 1 to Log4j 2 migration guide, and specifically the section on eliminating reliance on the bridge.

References

  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-34479

entry.title: [org.keycloak:keycloak-services] Keycloak: Unauthorized access via improper validation of encrypted SAML assertions
entry.content:
Keycloak's SAML broker endpoint does not properly validate encrypted assertions when the overall SAML response is not signed. An attacker with a valid signed SAML assertion can exploit this by crafting a malicious SAML response, injecting an encrypted assertion for an arbitrary principal, leading to unauthorized access and potential information disclosure.

entry.title: [org.apache.tomcat:tomcat-util] Apache Tomcat util accepted misconfigured CRLs
entry.content:
Detection of Error Condition Without Action vulnerability in Apache Tomcat when configuring Certificate Revocation List (CRLs) for a FFM based connector. If an FFM connector was configured with invalid CRLs, the invalid CRLs were ignored meaning invalid certificates could be accepted.

This issue affects Apache Tomcat: from 11.0.0-M1 through 11.0.22, from 10.1.0-M7 through 10.1.55, from 9.0.83 through 9.0.118.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 11.0.23, 10.1.56 or 9.0.119, which fixes the issue.
